coastal-bc.label: Coastal BC
coastal-bc.oneLiner: Mild, wet winters and summer heat waves: fix moisture first, then cooling and heat pumps.
coastal-bc.summary: Coastal BC has Canada's mildest winters, but heavy rain from fall to spring soaks walls and roofs, and summer heat waves are now a health risk. Heating needs are the lowest of any region we cover, so damp, drafts and overheating are the common complaints. An EnerGuide evaluation here should look for moisture problems before any air sealing or insulation, then plan a heat pump that heats and cools.
drivers: Winters are long but mild: temperatures rarely drop below about −4°C to −8°C, so heat pumps run efficiently nearly all winter.
Wet winters: heavy rain from October to March soaks walls and roofs, and new homes here must have a rainscreen behind the siding.
Summers are dry, and heat waves are now a health risk in homes without cooling.
Most homes heat with electricity or gas, and power is relatively cheap (about 12.6¢/kWh in Vancouver, 2025), which favours heat pumps.

priorities.title: Fix moisture before tightening up
priorities.why: Heavy winter rain soaks walls and roofs here. Insulation makes outer layers colder and slower to dry, so fix leaks, condensation and mould first, or upgrades can trap water.
priorities.ask: Ask the registered energy advisor to note stains, damp spots and roof or window leaks, and to check that bath and kitchen fans vent outdoors.

priorities.title: Plan cooling before the next heat wave
priorities.why: Heat waves are now a real health risk on the coast. Health authorities recommend efficient active cooling, such as a ductless heat pump, so at least one room stays cool.
priorities.ask: Ask which rooms overheat and what it would take to cool them, especially top floors and rooms with large west- or south-facing windows.

priorities.title: Plan the switch to a heat pump
priorities.why: Almost all winter heating here happens at temperatures where heat pumps work efficiently, and one system can replace baseboards or a gas furnace and add cooling.
priorities.ask: Ask for a heat-loss calculation, and get your electrical panel checked early; NRCan notes electrical upgrades can take up to a year.

priorities.title: Seal air leaks, then top up the attic
priorities.why: NRCan calls air sealing the most important retrofit. Pair it with attic insulation: today's new-home minimum here is about R-39, a useful target for older attics.
priorities.ask: Ask for a blower door test before and after sealing, so you can see the drop in ACH50.

priorities.title: Add ventilation as you tighten
priorities.why: A tighter house in a damp climate needs fans or an HRV to keep winter humidity down. Without them, condensation and mould can follow, and gas appliances risk backdrafting.
priorities.ask: Ask for a ventilation assessment, and a combustion safety test if you have a gas furnace, boiler, water heater or fireplace.

priorities.title: Get ready for smoky days
priorities.why: Smoke reaches the coast too: Vancouver logged 171 hours of smoke and haze in September 2020. A good filter or air cleaner lets you keep windows shut.
priorities.ask: Ask whether your furnace or air handler can take a MERV 13 filter, or which certified portable air cleaner suits your main living area.

tests.why: Measures how leaky the house is (ACH50) and helps find leaks; testing before and after air sealing shows what the work achieved.
tests.when: Any season, ideally on a calm day.

tests.why: Shows missing insulation and air leaks as temperature differences on walls and ceilings.
tests.when: December to February, early morning or evening, with at least 10°C between inside and outside, little sun and low wind.

tests.why: Checks insulation depth and looks for damp or stained roof sheathing, a sign of roof leaks or warm, moist air escaping into the attic.
tests.when: During or just after the October-to-March rainy season, when wetting is at its peak.

tests.why: Checks that bath and kitchen fans vent outdoors and move enough air to control winter damp in a tighter house.
tests.when: At the same visit as the blower door test.

tests.why: Coastal radon is usually low, but a long-term test is the only way to know your home's level.
tests.when: At least 91 days, mostly in fall and winter, on the lowest floor you use.

upgrades.title: Heat pump in place of baseboards or gas
upgrades.why: One system heats and cools. Mild coastal winters keep it in its efficient range most of the time, and it uses much less electricity than baseboard heaters.
upgrades.note: Size it for both heating and cooling; an oversized unit short-cycles.

upgrades.title: Air sealing plus attic insulation
upgrades.why: Usually the best envelope value for the money. Aim for at least today's new-home attic level here, about R-39.
upgrades.note: Fix roof leaks and attic moisture before adding insulation.

upgrades.title: Quiet continuous exhaust fans or an HRV
upgrades.why: Keeps winter humidity in check once the house is tighter. An HRV brings in fresh air and recovers much of the heat from stale air going out.
upgrades.note: In most coastal homes an HRV is a better fit than an ERV.

upgrades.title: Shading for hot, sunny rooms
upgrades.why: Exterior shades, awnings and trees cut summer heat gain at low cost. Close coverings on sunny windows by day, and ventilate at night when it's cooler outside.
upgrades.note: On smoky days, keep windows closed and rely on filtration instead.

upgrades.title: Better filtration for smoke days
upgrades.why: A MERV 13 filter in the furnace or air handler, or a certified portable air cleaner, keeps indoor air cleaner when wildfire smoke drifts in.
upgrades.note: Check that your system's fan and filter slot can handle a higher-rated filter.

equipment: A standard variable-speed heat pump can usually heat the whole house here. A cold-climate heat pump adds margin for Arctic outflow cold snaps like January 2024's.
Baseboards can stay as backup heat and run alongside the heat pump. Set their thermostats 2–3°C below the heat pump's setting so it does most of the work.
Ask for sizing that balances heating and cooling. An oversized unit short-cycles, wastes energy and keeps rooms less comfortable.
For ventilation, an HRV usually suits damp coastal homes better than an ERV, which NRCan suggests mainly where cooling loads are high or indoor air runs dry.
health: Winter damp: indoor relative humidity above about 40% in cold weather can cause window condensation, staining and mould. Run bath and kitchen fans, and fix leaks promptly.
Heat safety: in the 2021 heat dome, 98% of BC's heat deaths happened indoors, mostly in homes without adequate cooling. Make sure at least one room can be kept cool.
Smoky days: keep windows closed, limit exhaust fans and run filtration. If heat and smoke arrive together and it's too hot indoors, staying cool comes first.
Radon is low on the coast: the 2024 national survey found about 1 in 75 homes at or above 200 Bq/m³. Test anyway; it's the only way to know.

avoid.title: Insulating walls before fixing rain leaks
avoid.why: In this wet climate, insulation and interior vapour barriers can trap water in walls that leak. Fix the leak and make sure the wall can dry first.

avoid.title: Air sealing without adding ventilation
avoid.why: A tighter house without fans or an HRV holds more moisture, which leads to condensation and mould.

avoid.title: Assuming a mild climate means no cooling
avoid.why: Heat waves are now a health risk on the coast. Plan cooling before the next one, not during it.

avoid.title: Oversizing a heat pump to be safe
avoid.why: An oversized unit short-cycles, wastes energy and wears faster. Ask for a heat-loss calculation instead of a rule of thumb.

coastal-bc.seasonNote: Book the evaluation between October and March, when rain shows where moisture gets in and cold mornings suit thermal scans. Start a 3-month radon test in fall, and get cooling installed before summer.

bc-southern-interior.label: BC Southern Interior
bc-southern-interior.oneLiner: Hot, smoky summers and cold winters: plan cooling, filtration and heating together.
bc-southern-interior.summary: The Okanagan and Thompson valleys have cold winters and the hottest summer afternoons and driest air of any region we cover. Wildfire smoke often keeps windows shut in summer, and radon levels are among the highest in Canada. An EnerGuide evaluation here should cover heating, cooling, smoke filtration and a radon test together.
drivers: Two real seasons: winter cold snaps reach about −17°C to −23°C, and July afternoons average about 29°C.
Heat can be extreme: Kamloops had 62 days above 30°C in 2023, against a historical average of 33.
Wildfire smoke keeps windows closed for long stretches, so cooling and filtration run more; Kamloops logged a record 478 smoky hours in 2021.
Natural gas heats about 9 in 10 homes in the Kamloops area and 6 in 10 around Kelowna (2023).

priorities.title: Keep smoke out: seal leaks, filter well
priorities.why: When smoke rolls in, windows stay shut. A tighter house with a good filter keeps indoor air cleaner; Health Canada advises the highest-rated filter your system can handle.
priorities.ask: Ask the advisor where outside air leaks in, and whether your furnace or air handler can take a MERV 13 filter.

priorities.title: Size cooling and heating together
priorities.why: Long hot spells mean a heat pump has to handle summer cooling as well as winter heat. Equipment sized for only one season can leave you uncomfortable in the other.
priorities.ask: Ask for a room-by-room heat-loss calculation that also covers cooling, before you collect heat pump quotes.

priorities.title: Test for radon
priorities.why: About 1 in 3 homes across the BC Interior tested at or above Health Canada's 200 Bq/m³ guideline in the 2024 national survey, and Kelowna was among the highest municipalities.
priorities.ask: Start a 3-month radon test in the heating season, and retest after air sealing or basement work.

priorities.title: Seal and insulate the attic
priorities.why: Attic air sealing and insulation cut winter heat loss and summer heat gain. Today's new-home minimum here is about R-49, a useful target for older attics.
priorities.ask: Ask for an attic inspection that checks insulation depth and air leaks around light fixtures, the hatch and plumbing stacks.

priorities.title: Check your home's wildfire exposure
priorities.why: In August 2023, nearly 200 structures were destroyed or damaged in West Kelowna, Westbank First Nation and Kelowna. An energy audit doesn't cover wildfire risk, so ask separately.
priorities.ask: Ask your local fire department or FireSmart program about a home wildfire assessment.

tests.why: Measures leakage (ACH50), the paths that let smoke and hot air in.
tests.when: Any season, on a calm day.

tests.why: Finds missing insulation and air leaks.
tests.when: December to February, on cold mornings with little sun and wind; summer scans with air conditioning running are less reliable.

tests.why: Many comfort complaints are duct or airflow problems rather than undersized equipment, and the filter slot limits how well you can filter smoke.
tests.when: Before choosing a heat pump.

tests.why: Regional radon is high, and air sealing can change indoor levels.
tests.when: At least 91 days, mostly in the heating season; retest the next heating season after upgrades.

tests.why: Most homes here burn natural gas, and tightening the house can cause backdrafting of furnaces and water heaters.
tests.when: With the blower door test, and again after air sealing.

upgrades.title: Cold-climate heat pump paired with the furnace
upgrades.why: It gives efficient cooling and handles most winter heating, while the gas furnace covers the coldest nights. Hybrid controls switch fuels by outdoor temperature and energy price.
upgrades.note: Ask how the switchover is set; factory settings may not suit your rates.

upgrades.title: Air sealing plus attic insulation
upgrades.why: Cuts heating, cooling and smoke infiltration in one job. Aim for at least today's new-home attic level here, about R-49.

upgrades.title: MERV 13 filtration and a portable air cleaner
upgrades.why: Long fire seasons make good filtration important. A MERV 13 filter in the air handler plus a certified portable air cleaner helps you keep one room's air cleaner.
upgrades.note: Your system may need a fan check or wider filter slot first.

upgrades.title: Radon mitigation if your test is high
upgrades.why: If a long-term test is above 200 Bq/m³, Health Canada advises reducing it. A C-NRPP certified professional can install a sub-slab system.
upgrades.note: Retest after mitigation and after major air sealing.

upgrades.title: ERV for balanced ventilation
upgrades.why: Once the house is tighter, an ERV brings in fresh air while recovering heat, and it helps keep dry winter air from getting drier.

equipment: Choose a cold-climate heat pump with published capacity at your local design temperature (−17°C to −23°C), and keep backup heat. Many newer units stop running between −15°C and −25°C.
Keeping the gas furnace for the coldest weather (a hybrid system) is practical here, since most homes already have gas.
Cooling is a real load here: ask for sizing that covers both seasons, and avoid oversized equipment that short-cycles.
Summer air here is dry, so dehumidification is rarely the concern; an ERV is a sensible ventilation choice.
health: Smoky days: keep windows and doors closed, limit exhaust fans and run filtration. If it's too hot indoors with the windows shut, go to a cooler, cleaner-air space.
Radon: about 1 in 3 homes across the BC Interior and Yukon tested at or above 200 Bq/m³ in the 2024 survey, one of Canada's two highest regions.
Dry winter air: humidify modestly. Too much moisture causes window condensation and can dampen the attic.
Heat safety: summers bring long hot spells, so make sure at least one room can be kept cool.

avoid.title: Relying on open windows to cool the house
avoid.why: In smoke season, open windows let smoke in. Plan for mechanical cooling instead.

avoid.title: A standard heat pump with no backup heat
avoid.why: Cold snaps of −20°C and below can exceed what standard units deliver. Keep the furnace or another backup.

avoid.title: Skipping the radon retest after air sealing
avoid.why: Tightening a house can change radon levels. Retest in the next heating season.

avoid.title: Oversizing cooling equipment
avoid.why: Oversized units short-cycle, waste energy and leave rooms less comfortable.

bc-southern-interior.seasonNote: Book the evaluation in winter (December to February suits thermal scans), and start a 3-month radon test in fall. Get cooling and filtration in place before summer smoke season.

prairies.label: Prairies
prairies.oneLiner: Long, very cold, very dry winters: air sealing, radon testing and humidity balance lead.
prairies.summary: Heating is the big bill here: winters are long and very dry, and cold snaps reach −30°C to −35°C. Radon is common, and electricity prices vary widely between provinces, which changes what pays back. An EnerGuide evaluation should focus on air sealing, attic and basement insulation, a radon test and safe humidity levels.
drivers: Heating dominates: winters are long, and cold snaps regularly reach −30°C to −35°C.
Winter air is extremely dry, so homes feel parched, yet over-humidifying frosts windows and can wet the attic.
Natural gas heats 70% to 83% of homes in Alberta and Saskatchewan cities, and 56% in Winnipeg (2023).
Power prices differ sharply: about 23¢/kWh in Calgary, 18¢ in Regina and 10.5¢ in Winnipeg (April 2025), which shapes heat-pump savings.

priorities.title: Seal the top and bottom of the house
priorities.why: In deep cold, warm air rises and escapes through attic leaks while cold air is pulled in down low. Sealing both saves heat and helps prevent attic frost and ice dams.
priorities.ask: Ask the registered energy advisor to find attic bypasses, rim joist gaps and basement penetrations during the blower door test.

priorities.title: Test every home for radon
priorities.why: The 2024 national survey found about 1 in 3 homes at or above Health Canada's guideline in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and just over 1 in 6 in Alberta.
priorities.ask: Run a 3-month test in the heating season, then retest after air sealing or basement work.

priorities.title: Balance dry air against condensation
priorities.why: Winter air is extremely dry, but humidifying too much frosts windows and can wet walls and attic sheathing. The colder it gets outside, the lower indoor humidity must be.
priorities.ask: Ask for a ventilation assessment and a target indoor relative humidity that suits your windows and outdoor temperatures.

priorities.title: Insulate the basement and rim joists
priorities.why: Basements can account for about 20% of a home's heat loss. Check for cracks and water entry first; Manitoba's clay soils cracked some foundations during the 2021 drought.
priorities.ask: Ask whether the basement is dry enough to insulate from inside, and how much air leaks at the rim joist.

priorities.title: Check gas appliances after tightening
priorities.why: Most homes here burn natural gas. Air sealing can depressurize the house and pull exhaust back inside, so appliances need a combustion safety test and working CO alarms.
priorities.ask: Ask for a combustion safety test during the blower door visit, and again after air sealing.

tests.why: Measures leakage and, with a thermal scan, pinpoints attic bypasses and rim joist and window leaks.
tests.when: Any season; most revealing with a thermal scan on a cold, calm day.

tests.why: Deep cold makes missing insulation and air leaks stand out clearly.
tests.when: November to March, avoiding sunny walls and windy days.

tests.why: Frost, damp sheathing or thin insulation in the attic point to warm air leaking up from the house below.
tests.when: Mid-winter, after a cold spell.

tests.why: High-radon region, and energy upgrades can change indoor levels.
tests.when: At least 91 days in the heating season, on the lowest floor you use.

tests.why: Checks that gas furnaces and water heaters vent safely in a tighter house.
tests.when: During the blower door visit, especially after air sealing.

upgrades.title: Attic air sealing, then insulation to R-59
upgrades.why: Seal attic bypasses first, then insulate to at least today's new-home level for most of the region, about R-59. It cuts heat loss and helps prevent ice dams.
upgrades.note: Lethbridge's new-home level is a little lower, about R-49.

upgrades.title: Basement wall and rim joist insulation
upgrades.why: A big share of heat loss in a long heating season. Fix water entry first; never insulate a wet basement from the inside.

upgrades.title: High-efficiency furnace or a hybrid heat pump
upgrades.why: Where gas is the main fuel and power costs more, a cold-climate heat pump paired with the gas furnace often makes sense. Winnipeg's low power prices favour using the heat pump more.
upgrades.note: Ask how the switchover settings are configured for your rates.

upgrades.title: Balanced ventilation with an HRV or ERV
upgrades.why: Once the house is tight, balanced ventilation controls moisture and stale air. An ERV can help keep very dry houses from drying out further.

equipment: Heating fully with a heat pump here generally needs a cold-climate heat pump, and backup heat is still required below its cut-off; cold-climate models work to about −30°C.
Hybrid (dual-fuel) systems that keep the gas furnace for the coldest weather are a practical choice where power costs more, as in Alberta.
Ground-source heat pumps avoid defrost and stay efficient in the coldest months, but their payback depends heavily on local power rates and the fuel replaced.
Cooling is worthwhile in Winnipeg and Regina, where summers bring regular hot spells; much of Alberta needs little. An ERV often suits these dry-winter homes better than an HRV.
health: Radon: the 2024 national survey found about 1 in 5 homes at or above 200 Bq/m³ across the Prairies and NWT, and close to 1 in 3 in Saskatchewan and Manitoba.
Wildfire smoke is a recurring summer issue: Calgary logged 512 smoky hours in 2021, and Saskatoon, Regina and Winnipeg had their smokiest July on record in 2025.
Dry indoor air: relative humidity of 20% or more helps comfort, but the safe limit drops as it gets colder outside; above it, windows frost.
Extreme cold: protect pipes in exterior walls and unheated spaces, and keep CO alarms working near gas appliances.

avoid.title: Over-humidifying in deep cold
avoid.why: It frosts windows and can wet attic sheathing and walls.

avoid.title: A standard heat pump with no backup heat
avoid.why: It can't be expected to carry −30°C nights. Keep the furnace or another backup.

avoid.title: Sealing around gas appliances without a safety check
avoid.why: A tighter house can pull exhaust back inside. Get a combustion safety test and keep CO alarms working.

avoid.title: Chopping ice dams off the roof
avoid.why: An axe or pick damages the roof. Ice dams come from attic air leaks and thin insulation, so fix those instead.

prairies.seasonNote: Book the evaluation between November and March, when cold weather makes air leaks and missing insulation easy to see. Start a 3-month radon test in the heating season, and check the attic after a cold spell.

great-lakes-st-lawrence.label: Great Lakes–St. Lawrence
great-lakes-st-lawrence.oneLiner: Cold winters and hot, humid summers: seal the attic, dry the basement, plan cooling.
great-lakes-st-lawrence.summary: This region has real winters and hot, humid summers, so bills come from both heating and cooling. Natural gas heats most Ontario homes, while most Quebec homes use low-cost electricity. An EnerGuide evaluation here should cover air sealing and the attic, cooling and dehumidification, and keeping the basement dry before insulating it.
drivers: Both seasons cost money: winters are cold, and summers bring 37 to 74 days a year with a humidex of 30 or more.
Gas heats 50% to 85% of homes in Ontario cities; in Quebec most homes use electric heat, and 16% already heat with heat pumps.
Electricity costs about 8.3¢/kWh in Montreal versus 14.4¢ in Ottawa and 15.6¢ in Toronto (April 2025), which shapes heat-pump savings.
Basement flooding is a growing cost: 2024 storms flooded basements from Toronto to Montreal, with insured losses in the billions.

priorities.title: Seal air leaks and top up the attic
priorities.why: Air sealing is still the first retrofit. In the snowier Ottawa–Montreal–Sherbrooke belt, a leaky, under-insulated attic also causes ice dams.
priorities.ask: Ask for a blower door test and attic inspection, and whether old vermiculite insulation needs testing before any attic work.

priorities.title: Right-size cooling to control humidity
priorities.why: In humid summers, an oversized air conditioner or heat pump cools quickly but shuts off before removing moisture, leaving rooms clammy. A heat pump replacing the air conditioner also covers much of the heating.
priorities.ask: Ask for a room-by-room heat-loss calculation and a duct and airflow check before replacing your air conditioner or furnace.

priorities.title: Keep the basement dry before insulating
priorities.why: Basements can be about 20% of heat loss, but insulating a damp basement from the inside can rot the new wall. Flash floods have hit Toronto and Montreal repeatedly.
priorities.ask: Ask the advisor to check grading, downspouts, foundation cracks and the sump, and to look for damp spots or white mineral stains.

priorities.title: Test for radon
priorities.why: About 1 in 6 homes in the Ottawa–Gatineau and Montreal areas tested at or above Health Canada's guideline in the 2024 survey; Kingston and Sherbrooke ranked among the highest municipalities.
priorities.ask: Run a 3-month test in the heating season, and retest after air sealing or basement work.

priorities.title: Plan backup heat for power outages
priorities.why: Recent ice storms and the May 2022 derecho windstorm each left hundreds of thousands of customers without power. Every heat-pump plan needs backup heat and a safe way through an outage.
priorities.ask: Ask how your home would stay warm in an outage, and keep baseboards or the furnace as backup when adding a heat pump.

tests.why: Measures leakage (ACH50) and, with a thermal scan, finds where air gets in.
tests.when: Any season; pair it with a thermal scan in winter.

tests.why: Shows missing insulation and air leaks as cold spots.
tests.when: December to February, early morning or on an overcast day, with at least 10°C between inside and outside.

tests.why: Prevents oversized equipment that short-cycles and dehumidifies poorly, and is needed to choose the right heat pump.
tests.when: Before replacing an air conditioner or furnace, based on the house after planned upgrades.

tests.why: Moderate to high regional radon, and upgrades can change indoor levels.
tests.when: At least 91 days, mostly in the heating season; retest after upgrades.

tests.why: In gas-heated homes, tightening can cause spillage from older furnaces and water heaters.
tests.when: During the blower door visit.

upgrades.title: Air sealing plus attic insulation
upgrades.why: Usually the best envelope payback. Today's new-home attic minimum here is about R-49, a good target for older homes.
upgrades.note: Don't disturb old vermiculite insulation until it's tested for asbestos.

upgrades.title: Heat pump instead of a new air conditioner
upgrades.why: One machine gives efficient cooling and most of the heating. In Ontario it often pairs with the gas furnace; in Quebec, baseboards can stay as backup.
upgrades.note: Choose a cold-climate model in colder cities such as Ottawa, Montreal and Sherbrooke.

upgrades.title: Basement insulation, once it's dry
upgrades.why: A large heat-loss area. Fix water entry first, then insulate.

upgrades.title: Covered sump and better drainage
upgrades.why: NRCan lists a covered sump among basement moisture fixes. Extending downspouts and sloping soil away from the house help keep storm water out.

upgrades.title: ERV for balanced ventilation
upgrades.why: Brings in fresh air while recovering heat; NRCan suggests ERVs where cooling loads are high, as they are here.

equipment: In colder cities such as Ottawa, Montreal and Sherbrooke, choose a cold-climate heat pump. Along Lakes Erie and Ontario, good variable-speed units cover most hours, with backup heat.
When a heat pump replaces the air conditioner, size it to balance heating and cooling; NRCan's guide caps cooling capacity at about 125% of the cooling load.
Electric backup (baseboards or strips) can run with the heat pump; a furnace in a hybrid system takes over instead of running at the same time.
For dehumidification, run the indoor fan on low in cooling mode, and size equipment so it runs long cycles.
health: Damp basements: run a dehumidifier in summer, and keep indoor relative humidity below about 40% in cold weather to avoid condensation and mould.
Wildfire smoke can travel far: Ottawa's fine-particle level hit 511 on June 7, 2023 (normal is 4 to 11), and Montreal briefly had the world's worst air that month.
Heat: Ottawa reached a humidex of 47 in the 2018 Canada Day heat wave. Make sure at least one room can be kept cool.
Radon: about 1 in 6 homes across Central Canada tested at or above 200 Bq/m³ in the 2024 survey, though only about 1 in 22 in the Toronto area.

avoid.title: Insulating a damp basement from the inside
avoid.why: Trapped moisture rots the new wall and feeds mould. Fix drainage and leaks first.

avoid.title: An oversized air conditioner or heat pump
avoid.why: It short-cycles, removes less humidity and wears out faster.

avoid.title: Tightening a gas-heated home without a safety test
avoid.why: Older gas appliances can spill exhaust into a tighter house. Ask for a combustion safety test.

avoid.title: Leaving hybrid controls on factory settings
avoid.why: The switchover between heat pump and furnace should match your gas and electricity prices. Ask how it's set.

great-lakes-st-lawrence.seasonNote: Book the evaluation in winter (December to February) for clear thermal scans, and start a 3-month radon test in fall. Check the basement after spring thaw or heavy rain, and line up cooling work before summer.

very-cold-east.label: Very Cold East
very-cold-east.oneLiner: Deep, snowy winters: stop ice dams, and pair a cold-climate heat pump with backup heat.
very-cold-east.summary: Winters here are long and deep, with cold snaps of −25°C to −31°C and the heaviest snow loads of any region we cover. Heat escaping into the attic melts roof snow from below, which refreezes as ice dams. An EnerGuide evaluation here should focus on the attic, the basement and rim joists, and a heating plan with reliable backup heat.
drivers: Long, deep heating season: cold snaps reach −25°C to −31°C.
Snow lies 10 cm or deeper on the ground for 99 to 134 days a year, so attic heat leaks readily form ice dams.
Electric heat serves 76% to 78% of homes around Saguenay and Quebec City; gas heats 74% in Sudbury and 81% in Thunder Bay.
Summers are mild but can be humid, with about 23 to 31 days a year at a humidex of 30 or more.

priorities.title: Stop ice dams at the attic
priorities.why: NRCan says the best way to prevent ice dams is sealing attic air leaks and insulating thoroughly, so roof snow stays frozen. Snow loads here are the heaviest of any region we cover.
priorities.ask: Ask the advisor to trace attic bypasses with the blower door and thermal camera, and to check insulation depth.

priorities.title: Cold-climate heat pump with reliable backup
priorities.why: Cold snaps of −25°C to −31°C are at or beyond many heat pumps' limits, so backup heat is a must: baseboards in most Quebec homes, the furnace in Ontario.
priorities.ask: Ask for a heat-loss calculation and a heat pump with published capacity near −25°C to −30°C.

priorities.title: Insulate the basement and rim joists
priorities.why: Basements can be about 20% of a home's heat loss, and the long cold season makes the savings add up. Rim joists are often among the leakiest spots.
priorities.ask: Ask whether the basement is dry enough to insulate from inside, and how much the rim joist leaks.

priorities.title: Test for radon
priorities.why: Thunder Bay ranked among the highest municipalities in the 2024 national survey, and about 1 in 6 Quebec homes tested at or above Health Canada's guideline.
priorities.ask: Run a 3-month test in the heating season, and retest after air sealing.

priorities.title: Ventilate and keep humidity in check
priorities.why: Winter air is very dry, but humidifying too much frosts windows and wets the attic. Balanced ventilation keeps a tighter house fresh without adding moisture problems.
priorities.ask: Ask for a ventilation assessment and the indoor relative humidity your windows can handle in deep cold.

tests.why: Finds the attic and rim joist leaks that feed ice dams.
tests.when: Any season; most useful with a thermal scan in winter.

tests.why: Shows missing insulation and air leaks clearly in the cold.
tests.when: November to March, on calm days with little sun on the walls being scanned.

tests.why: Frost, wet sheathing and roof melt patterns show where heat escapes; watch where snow melts first after a light snowfall.
tests.when: Early winter, after the first light snow or a heavy frost.

tests.why: Regional radon risk, and air sealing can change indoor levels.
tests.when: At least 91 days in the heating season.

tests.why: In gas-heated Ontario homes, tightening can make appliances spill exhaust.
tests.when: During the blower door visit.

upgrades.title: Attic air sealing and insulation to R-59
upgrades.why: Today's new-home attic minimum here is about R-59. Sealing first, then insulating, is the best way to prevent ice dams.
upgrades.note: Have old vermiculite insulation tested for asbestos before disturbing it.

upgrades.title: Cold-climate heat pump, keeping your backup
upgrades.why: Cold-climate units work to about −30°C and use much less electricity than baseboards; keep baseboards or the furnace for the coldest nights.

upgrades.title: Basement and rim joist insulation
upgrades.why: A large heat-loss area over a long season. Fix any dampness before insulating from inside.

upgrades.title: HRV or ERV for balanced ventilation
upgrades.why: Controls humidity and air quality once the house is tighter.

equipment: Choose a cold-climate heat pump with published capacity near −25°C to −30°C, and keep full backup heat for colder nights.
Set electric backup 2–3°C below the heat pump's setting so the heat pump does most of the work.
Look for demand-defrost controls, which are generally more efficient; ground-source heat pumps need no defrost at all.
Cooling needs are modest, but humid spells make a heat pump's cooling a welcome bonus.
health: Radon: about 1 in 8 Ontario homes and 1 in 6 Quebec homes tested at or above 200 Bq/m³ in the 2024 survey. Test every home.
Dry indoor air in deep cold: keep relative humidity within what your windows can handle without frosting.
Carbon monoxide: put CO alarms near every fuel-burning appliance and outside sleeping areas.
Heavy summer rain happens too: Quebec City had its wettest July in 150 years in 2023, so check basement drainage.

avoid.title: Chopping ice dams with an axe or pick
avoid.why: It damages the roof. Fix the attic air leaks and insulation that cause them.

avoid.title: Heat pumps without backup heat
avoid.why: Cold snaps here go beyond many units' cut-off. Keep baseboards or the furnace.

avoid.title: Over-humidifying in winter
avoid.why: It frosts windows and can wet attic sheathing.

avoid.title: Skipping the radon retest after tightening
avoid.why: Air sealing can change radon levels; retest in the next heating season.

atlantic.label: Atlantic Canada
atlantic.oneLiner: Damp, windy, icy winters and costly oil: switch to heat pumps, seal, test for radon.
atlantic.summary: Atlantic winters are wet, windy and icy rather than extremely cold, and summers are mild. Heating oil is still common and its price rose sharply in 2026, while heat pumps already heat many homes. An EnerGuide evaluation here should plan the move off oil, seal wind-driven leaks, fix moisture before insulating, and include a radon test.
drivers: Wind drives heat out: damp, windy winters push cold air through gaps in the house, and freezing rain is frequent.
Oil still heats 28% of homes in Nova Scotia and PEI; heat pumps heat 31% in NS, about 41% in PEI and 48% in NB.
Heating oil jumped 65% to 81% in a year: by September 2026 it averaged about $2.00 to $2.60 a litre in Atlantic cities.
Electricity costs about 15.6¢/kWh in St. John's to 20.5¢ in Halifax (April 2025).

priorities.title: Plan your move off oil
priorities.why: Oil prices rose 65% to 81% in a year, and corrosion is a leading cause of oil tank leaks. Cold-climate heat pumps can be up to three times as efficient as oil heating.
priorities.ask: Ask the advisor to note your oil tank's age and condition, and to size a cold-climate heat pump with a backup plan.

priorities.title: Seal wind-driven leaks and the attic
priorities.why: Wind pushes cold air through gaps, and heavy, wet snow with frequent freezing rain makes a leaky attic prone to ice dams.
priorities.ask: Ask for a blower door test on a calm day, with a thermal scan to find wind-driven leaks.

priorities.title: Fix moisture before you insulate
priorities.why: Halifax, St. John's, Saint John and Charlottetown get enough wind-driven rain that new walls must have a rainscreen. Stop water getting into walls and basements before adding insulation.
priorities.ask: Ask the advisor to check the basement, attic sheathing and walls under windows for damp, and how bath fans vent.

priorities.title: Test for radon
priorities.why: Atlantic Canada had the highest radon of any region in the 2024 national survey: about 1 in 3 homes at or above Health Canada's guideline, and more than 1 in 3 in Nova Scotia.
priorities.ask: Run a 3-month test in the heating season, and retest after air sealing or other upgrades.

priorities.title: Plan for storms and power outages
priorities.why: Dorian in 2019 affected 80% of Nova Scotia Power customers, and Fiona in 2022 cut power to over 600,000 homes and businesses. Keep backup heat until a heat pump has proven itself.
priorities.ask: Ask where the outdoor unit should sit to stay clear of drifting snow and ice, and how you'd heat during an outage.

tests.why: Finds wind-driven leakage paths; a before-and-after test shows what sealing achieved.
tests.when: December to March, on a calm day.

tests.why: Shows insulation gaps and air leaks.
tests.when: December to March, on a calm, overcast day with at least 10°C between inside and outside.

tests.why: Checks that the oil burner and chimney vent safely, especially once air sealing changes indoor air pressure.
tests.when: Before winter, and again after air sealing.

tests.why: Damp air and heavy rain make moisture the main risk; this checks fans, indoor humidity and signs of mould.
tests.when: Late fall or the spring wet season.

tests.why: High regional radon.
tests.when: At least 91 days in the heating season; retest after upgrades.

upgrades.title: Cold-climate heat pump to replace oil or baseboards
upgrades.why: Ductless mini-splits or a ducted system cut heating costs and add summer cooling. They're already common: mini-splits heat 38% of homes in the Moncton area.
upgrades.note: Keep the oil system or baseboards as backup until the heat pump has handled a cold snap and an outage.

upgrades.title: Air sealing plus attic insulation
upgrades.why: Cuts wind-driven heat loss and helps prevent ice dams. Today's new-home attic minimum here is about R-49.

upgrades.title: Basement insulation after moisture control
upgrades.why: Basements can be about 20% of heat loss; dry the basement first, then insulate.

upgrades.title: HRV for balanced ventilation
upgrades.why: Removes winter moisture from a tighter house while recovering much of the heat.

upgrades.title: Replace a corroded oil tank, or remove it
upgrades.why: Corrosion is a leading cause of tank leaks, and spill cleanups are expensive and can affect resale.
upgrades.note: If you keep oil, check the tank and lines for leaks after each fill.

equipment: Use a cold-climate heat pump, and keep existing oil or electric baseboards as backup for cold snaps and outages.
If oil stays as backup, set its thermostat below the heat pump's so the heat pump does most of the work.
Choose demand-defrost controls, which NRCan says are generally more efficient than timed defrost.
An HRV usually suits damp coastal homes better than an ERV, which is suggested mainly for high cooling loads or dry indoor air.
health: Radon is a major hidden health risk here: the 2024 survey found about 1 in 3 Atlantic homes at or above 200 Bq/m³, the highest of any region.
Damp and mould: run bath and kitchen fans, and keep winter relative humidity low enough to avoid condensation.
Carbon monoxide: install CO alarms near oil appliances or a wood stove, and in each bedroom area.
Wildfire can reach city edges: the June 2023 Tantallon fire destroyed about 150 homes in the Halifax area.

avoid.title: Ignoring an old oil tank
avoid.why: Corrosion is a leading cause of leaks, and cleanups are expensive and can hurt resale.

avoid.title: Removing all backup heat too soon
avoid.why: Keep a backup until the heat pump has proven itself through a cold snap and a power outage.

avoid.title: Insulating a damp basement from the inside
avoid.why: Trapped moisture can rot new framing and feed mould. Fix water entry first.

avoid.title: Air sealing a damp house without ventilation
avoid.why: A tighter house holds more moisture; add fans or an HRV at the same time.

north.label: The North
north.oneLiner: Extreme cold and costly energy: envelope first, reliable heat, safe oil tanks, permafrost.
north.summary: The North has the longest, coldest winters we cover, with temperatures that reach −41°C. About half of Yukon homes heat with oil, and electricity costs more than in southern cities, so every bit of heat kept in saves real money. An EnerGuide evaluation here should put the building envelope first, then check heating reliability, oil tank safety, ventilation and humidity limits, and signs of permafrost movement.
drivers: The longest, coldest heating season we cover: cold snaps reach −41°C in both Whitehorse and Yellowknife.
Oil heats about half of Yukon homes, and heating oil averaged about $2.25 to $2.28 a litre in Whitehorse and Yellowknife in September 2026.
Electricity is expensive: about 26¢/kWh in Whitehorse, and well over 30¢ in Yellowknife once extra charges are added (2026).
Yukon's grid is mostly hydro, but liquefied natural gas and diesel cover winter peaks, so deep-winter heat-pump use partly runs on fossil power.

priorities.title: Envelope first: seal, insulate, upgrade windows
priorities.why: With the coldest winters we cover and costly fuel, envelope work saves more than equipment changes. Today's new-home minimums here, about R-59 attics and R-22 walls, are good targets.
priorities.ask: Ask for a blower door test with a thermal scan, and a list of envelope upgrades ranked by savings.

priorities.title: Keep heat reliable and oil tanks safe
priorities.why: Oil is the main fuel, and losing heat at −40°C is serious. Permafrost movement can tilt oil tanks and strain fuel lines.
priorities.ask: Ask the advisor to check the burner, venting and CO alarms, and to look for a leaning tank or bent supply line.

priorities.title: Ventilate within humidity limits
priorities.why: A tight house needs fresh air, but at −40°C indoor relative humidity must stay very low, about 12% to 20% depending on the windows, to avoid frost and condensation.
priorities.ask: Ask for a ventilation assessment, and an HRV or ERV with frost protection.

priorities.title: Watch for permafrost movement
priorities.why: Whitehorse sits where permafrost underlies 10% to 50% of the ground, and Yellowknife-area homes can sit on thaw-sensitive patches. Thaw can crack walls and jam doors.
priorities.ask: Ask the advisor to note sticking doors, new cracks or sloping floors, and call an engineer if the house is moving.

priorities.title: Test for radon
priorities.why: Whitehorse ranked among the highest municipalities in the 2024 national survey, and about 1 in 4 Yukon homes tested at or above Health Canada's guideline.
priorities.ask: Run a 3-month test in the heating season, and retest after air sealing.

tests.why: The biggest savings come from finding and sealing leaks; it measures ACH50 before and after.
tests.when: October to April, avoiding strong wind.

tests.why: Deep cold makes insulation gaps and air leaks stand out clearly.
tests.when: October to April, almost any day; avoid strong wind and sun on the walls being scanned.

tests.why: Oil and propane heat many homes, and a tighter house can cause backdrafting.
tests.when: With the blower door visit.

tests.why: Checks that fresh air reaches a tight house without pushing indoor humidity past what the windows can handle.
tests.when: In mid-winter, when humidity limits are tightest.

tests.why: High radon in Yukon.
tests.when: At least 91 days in the heating season.

upgrades.title: Air sealing and insulation to northern levels
upgrades.why: The biggest savings anywhere we cover: the highest heating demand, paid for with costly oil and power. Seal first, then insulate attics, walls and rim joists.

upgrades.title: Efficient heating with full backup
upgrades.why: A high-efficiency oil, propane or pellet system, or a cold-climate heat pump with full backup where power is mostly hydro. Air-source heat pumps can't carry the coldest weather here.

upgrades.title: HRV with frost protection
upgrades.why: Brings in fresh air without throwing away heat in a tight house.

upgrades.title: Energy-efficient windows
upgrades.why: Cut heat loss and let you keep a little more indoor humidity before windows frost.

equipment: Air-source heat pumps need a full-size backup here: in NRCan's subarctic zone, only about 45% of the yearly heating load comes at −9.4°C or warmer.
Cold-climate air-source heat pumps are rated to about −30°C, while cold snaps here reach −41°C.
An ERV suits homes where indoor air runs very dry, as it does in northern winters; whichever you choose, it needs frost protection.
Keep CO alarms near every fuel-burning appliance, and have oil burners serviced before winter.
health: Radon: about 1 in 4 Yukon homes and about 1 in 5 NWT homes tested at or above 200 Bq/m³ in the 2024 survey. Test every home.
Wildfire smoke and evacuation: about 20,000 people left Yellowknife and nearby communities for almost three weeks in August 2023. Have filtration ready for smoky days.
Extreme cold: Whitehorse fell to −44.8°C in January 2022. Protect pipes, and have a plan if the heat goes out.
Very dry indoor air: humidify only within window-condensation limits, or frost and moisture build up on windows and in walls.

avoid.title: Banking snow or water against the foundation
avoid.why: It warms the ground and can thaw permafrost under the house. Keep snow and drainage away from the foundation.

avoid.title: An air-source heat pump without full backup
avoid.why: It can't carry the coldest weather here.

avoid.title: Leaving oil tanks and lines unchecked
avoid.why: Ground movement can tilt tanks and bend supply hoses; check them every season.

avoid.title: Air sealing without ventilation and safety checks
avoid.why: A tight house needs fresh air and a combustion safety test so appliances vent safely.

About 28 days a year with wind chill below −30.
Permafrost underlies 10% to 50% of the ground; thaw can crack walls and shift tanks.
Radon: the 2024 survey listed Whitehorse among Canada's 18 highest municipalities.

windsor.note: Windsor has the hottest, most humid summers of any city we cover, with about 74 days a year at a humidex of 30 or more, so cooling and dehumidification drive comfort here. Mild winters let a good heat pump cover most heating hours.
hazards: Neighbouring LaSalle got 285 mm of rain in 32 hours in August 2017.
About 24 days a year above 30°C and 33 with a humidex of 35 or more.
About 2.5 days a year with wind gusts of 90 km/h or more.
Radon: about 1 in 8 Ontario homes tested at or above the guideline in 2024.

winnipeg.note: Winnipeg has some of the deepest cold we cover, with about 43 days a year of wind chill below −30, plus humid summers that make cooling worthwhile. Electricity is cheap (about 10.5¢/kWh), so a cold-climate heat pump can do more of the heating here.
hazards: Radon: the 2024 survey listed Winnipeg among Canada's 18 highest municipalities.
Wettest spring on record in 2022; the Red River neared 2009 flood levels.
138 mm of rain fell on the city's western edge on August 20, 2025.
Wildfire smoke: 239 smoky hours in 2021 and the smokiest July on record in 2025.

yellowknife.note: Yellowknife has the highest heating demand of any city we cover, with about 89 days a year of wind chill below −30, and power costs well over 30¢/kWh once extra charges are added. Envelope upgrades save more here than almost anywhere else.
hazards: About 20,000 people were evacuated for almost three weeks in August 2023 as wildfire approached.
Thaw-sensitive permafrost patches can shift houses, oil tanks and fuel lines.
Radon: about 1 in 5 NWT homes tested at or above the guideline in 2024.

alberta.note: Electricity is among Canada's priciest, about 23¢/kWh in Calgary and 22¢ in Edmonton (2025), while natural gas heats 76% of homes. A hybrid heat pump that keeps the gas furnace is often the practical choice. Calgary's hailstorms make roof checks worthwhile.
alberta.radon: Just over 1 in 6 Alberta homes tested at or above 200 Bq/m³ in the 2024 survey, about the same in the Calgary and Edmonton areas.

bc.note: BC has two very different climates: the mild, rainy coast and the hot, dry, often smoky Interior. Gas heats 42% of homes and electric heat, including heat pumps, about 47%. Electricity is relatively cheap, about 12.6¢/kWh in Vancouver (2025).
bc.radon: In the 2024 survey, about 1 in 75 coastal homes but about 1 in 3 Interior homes tested at or above 200 Bq/m³. Kelowna ranked among the highest municipalities.

manitoba.note: Electricity is among Canada's cheapest, about 10.5¢/kWh in Winnipeg (2025), so heat pumps compete well with gas, which heats 52% of homes. Winnipeg also has humid summers, river flood risk and clay soils that can crack foundations in drought.
manitoba.radon: About 1 in 3 homes tested at or above 200 Bq/m³ in the 2024 survey; Winnipeg and Brandon ranked among Canada's highest municipalities.

new-brunswick.note: Heat pumps are mainstream: 27% of homes heat with heat pumps and another 21% with mini-splits, while 39% use other electric heat and 6% wood. Electricity costs about 16.6¢/kWh in Moncton (2025), and the Saint John River floods in some springs.
new-brunswick.radon: About 1 in 4 homes tested at or above 200 Bq/m³ in the 2024 survey, and Bathurst ranked among Canada's highest municipalities. Test every home.

newfoundland-labrador.note: Most homes heat with electricity (64% baseboards or other electric heat, 20% heat pumps including mini-splits), and oil heats 13%; its price rose 81% in a year to $2.41 a litre in St. John's. St. John's averages about 31 freezing-rain days a year.
newfoundland-labrador.radon: About 1 in 5 homes tested at or above 200 Bq/m³ in the 2024 survey. Test every home with a 3-month test.

north.note: Oil heats about half of Yukon homes. Power costs about 26¢/kWh in Whitehorse and well over 30¢ in Yellowknife and many NWT communities. Permafrost, found throughout Nunavut and under parts of Whitehorse and Yellowknife, can shift houses and oil tanks.
north.radon: About 1 in 4 Yukon and 1 in 5 NWT homes tested at or above 200 Bq/m³ in the 2024 survey. Nunavut had too few results to report.

ontario.note: Natural gas heats 58% of homes, and electricity costs about 14¢ to 16¢/kWh in Ottawa and Toronto (2025). Southern Ontario has hot, humid summers and storm flooding; Northern Ontario has deep winters and heavy snow. Ice storms make backup heat worth planning.
ontario.radon: About 1 in 8 homes tested at or above 200 Bq/m³ in the 2024 survey: about 1 in 6 in Ottawa–Gatineau but 1 in 22 around Toronto.

pei.note: Heat pumps are now PEI's leading heat source (36% of homes, plus about 5% mini-splits), but oil still heats 28% and its price rose 69% in a year. Electricity costs about 19.7¢/kWh in Charlottetown (2025), and wood heats 8% of homes.
pei.radon: About 1 in 5 homes tested at or above 200 Bq/m³ in the 2024 survey. Test every home with a 3-month test.

quebec.note: Electricity heats most homes (70% with baseboards or other electric heat, 16% with heat pumps), and Hydro-Québec's rates are among North America's lowest, about 8.3¢/kWh in Montreal (2025). Ice storms, heavy rain and spring floods are the main weather hazards.
quebec.radon: About 1 in 6 homes tested at or above 200 Bq/m³ in the 2024 survey, including the Montreal area; Sherbrooke ranked among Canada's highest municipalities.

saskatchewan.note: Natural gas heats 75% of homes, and electricity costs about 17.9¢/kWh in Regina (2025). Winters are among the coldest in southern Canada, with cold snaps near −34°C to −35°C, and summers bring wildfire smoke and severe storms.
saskatchewan.radon: About 1 in 3 homes tested at or above 200 Bq/m³ in the 2024 survey, and Regina ranked among Canada's highest municipalities. Test every home.
